description_en: A stone pavilion from approx. 14th-15th century.The pavilion (baiṭhak) is situated in Ajayamerukoṭa, north-west of Amargadhi, Dadeldhura's current headquarters. The monument is found north of the Ḍo Gāḍ river, in the vicinity of the hill of the fortress of Ajayamerukoṭa (DDL0180) and a few meters to the north of a complex of śikhara temples (DDL0110,DDL0111,DDL0112and DDL0113). Next to the pavilion is a house occupied by a Nāth yogi.The area of Ajayamerukoṭa is rich in monuments that were mostly erected during the 14th and 15th centuries. According to D. P. Ojha, Ajayamerukoṭa was a local capital of the Khasiya kings from Jumla, (i.e. the Khaśa Malla emperors, 12th-14th century) (Ojha 1989: 54). From the mid-14th century, Ajayamerukoṭa seems to have taken greater importance as a capital of the Doti kingdom, especially under the reign of king Niraya Pāla (r. c. 1362-1383 CE). Indeed, it is around Niraya Pāla's time that Doti emerged as an independant entity. This political and economical rise is demonstrated in the numerous monuments erected between the second half of the 14th century and throughout the 15th century.Other pavilions were built in Ajayamerukoṭa, probably around the same time (DDL0050,DDL0140). This monument stands out from the others for its refinement and complexity. Twelve pillars (four on each side) support a doomed roof. Most of these elements are richly carved. The pillars display the traditional motifs of vase of holy water (Skt.kalaśa) and diamonds (Skt.ratna). The dome too is decorated, with each of its successive horizontal levels differenciated by different ornamental patterns. The two central pillars of the southern side are placed on a common platform. The bases of these pillars are decorated with representation of female dancers similar to the one seen on the nearby Setibada Baiṭhak (DDL005).D. R. Sharma estimates that the pavilion was built around the 12th-13th century (Sharma 2012, p. 314-317). While the monument indeed shares architectural features with construction such as the Baleśvara complex of Champawat (Uttarakhand, India), dated of ca. 1100-1250 by N. Chanchani (Chanchani 2019, p. 164-166) or some of themaṇḍapaof ca. 10th century temples inPadavali/Bateśvara(Madhya Pradesh, India), it also shows variations from these models. It is more likely that the pavilion was in fact built around the time of the rise of the Doti kingdom, i.e. in the second half of the 14th century.Ten meters east of the pavilion is a stone memorial pillar. The artefact does not show any inscription but may be attributed to the 14th-15th century. The south side contains a niche with the representation of a foot warrior holding a sword and a shield. Similarly, the western niche has a representation of a horse rider.
monument_assessment: Heavily damaged (collapsed, demolished, major cracks and structural damages), Surface damages, Structural damages
